name: Setting powder for photos (anti-shine)

lead: Skin shine shows up strongly in photos, especially under flash. A light dusting of face powder absorbs surface oil and mattes the forehead, nose and chin so the skin looks even and the highlights look controlled.
The effect is temporary and sits on the surface, but it is a quick way to look more polished on camera for anyone, including men who do not otherwise wear makeup.

paras: People apply loose or pressed translucent powder with a brush or puff, focusing on the T-zone, often over foundation or concealer or over plain moisturized skin. Blotting papers or a pressed compact are used for touch-ups. Some choose HD powders made for film and video.
Heavy use can look cakey, and powders can emphasise dry patches. Rarely, ingredients cause irritation; fragrance-free mineral versions exist.

chain: Skin looks even and matte in photos
angle.text: A thin layer of powder mattes oily areas so highlights do not blow out in photos. People use it for headshots, events and dating profile pictures.

lead: Setting powder is face powder used to set makeup, reduce shine and even out the skin's finish.[1] For photos, people use it to cut the shiny patches that cameras pick up on the forehead, nose and cheeks.

Face powders come loose or pressed. Loose powders are fine and give light coverage and oil absorption; pressed powders are compacted for touch-ups and give more coverage but can look cakey if overused.[1] Translucent powder is used to matte the skin, and HD powders were designed for film and video to reduce the white, flash-reflecting patches cameras can capture.[1]
infobox: Silica, starch, talc, kaolin, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide[1]
Temporary, until oil returns or it is wiped off

paras: Loose powder suits setting foundation and concealer; pressed powder suits touch-ups; mineral powder is made from ground minerals such as iron oxide, zinc and titanium dioxide and is typically free of fragrance and preservatives; finishing powder smooths the look of fine lines and pores.[1]

Face powder appears in ancient Egypt, and Greek, Roman and Chinese uses are documented; lead-based powders were common in Europe until the 16th century and zinc oxide powders became popular in the Victorian era.[1] Modern powders rarely contain toxic ingredients.[1]
